answer:
**Eulogy for Jason Wilson**

Good morning. On behalf of our family, thank you for being here. Thank you for taking a morning out of your lives to stand together in this room, in this particular quiet, for a man who spent sixty-seven years making other people's days a little easier.

Jason was my brother. And if you knew him at all, you know he would have hated all this fuss. He would have shifted in his chair. He would have made a joke to get the attention off himself. So let me apologize to him now, on all our behalf, and then let me go ahead and brag about him anyway — because he earned it, and because we need to say it out loud.

Jason passed away last Tuesday at Oakwood Medical Center. Sixty-seven years old. That number feels wrong in the mouth. It's too short for a man who filled a room the way he did, whose laugh you could find across a crowded hall, who could fix a screen door, listen to your troubles, and remember your kid's name all in the same afternoon.

He was the kind of brother who taught me things without ever sitting me down to teach them. How to shake a hand and look a person in the eye. How to be patient with someone who is learning. How to take a joke and, just as importantly, how not to take yourself too seriously. When we were young, our house was not a quiet place — and Jason was often at the center of whatever noise there was. He had a stubborn streak that could drive you half mad and a soft heart he tried to hide behind it. Most of us saw the stubbornness. If you were lucky, you got to see the heart.

That heart was the whole of him. Jason loved people in the plain, unglamorous way that actually matters. He showed up. He called when he said he would call. He remembered the thing you mentioned once, six months ago, and asked about it. He was not a man of grand speeches — heaven knows he'd be squirming through mine — but he was a man of small, steady kindnesses, and there were hundreds of them, and every one of them landed on somebody in this room.

Many of you knew him through his work. You knew the version of Jason who arrived early, who did the job properly, who never let a colleague carry the hard part alone. He believed that how you do your work is a statement about who you are, and he made that statement every single day. To his colleagues and friends here: he respected you. He talked about you. You were part of the fabric of his life, and he was proud to stand beside you.

And to those of you who cared for him at the end — the doctors and nurses and staff at Oakwood Medical Center — thank you. Thank you for your patience and your gentleness. Thank you for treating him like a person and not a chart. He noticed. He always noticed when someone was kind to him, and he never forgot it. Our family will not forget it either.

I want to say something to the younger people in this room, because Jason would want it said. He was not a man who measured a life in achievements. He measured it in relationships. In phone calls returned. In doors held open. In showing up for the ordinary Tuesday, not just the big occasions. If you take one thing from his life, take that. Be the person who shows up.

Grief is a strange, uneven thing. It will come at you sideways — in the sound of a certain song, a half-finished project, an unfamiliar silence where a familiar voice used to be. Some of you will feel it today; some of you will feel it three weeks from now in the cereal aisle. That's not weakness. That's just the size of what we've lost. And the size of it is the measure of how much he was loved.

So here is what I believe, and what I hold onto today: Jason is not gone from us. He is in the way we answer the phone. He is in the way we tell a story and can't help laughing at our own punchline. He is in every one of you who learned something from him — a skill, a habit of decency, a particular way of being kind without making a production of it. That is a legacy you cannot bury. We carry it out of this room with us, and we carry it for the rest of our lives.

Jason, my brother — you were stubborn, and funny, and generous, and far too modest about all of it. You did good work here. You were loved more than you ever let yourself believe. We will look after each other the way you would have wanted us to. We will tell your stories, and we will say your name, and we will keep you with us.

Rest easy now. The fuss is almost over — you'd be glad to hear it.

Thank you, everyone. Please, when you leave here today, call someone you love, and tell them plainly. Jason would call that a good use of a Tuesday.
